title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate drawn from a sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a margin of error — a statement about how wrong it might be.
Most people ignore it. In this assignment, you won’t.
In this analysis, I look at median gross rent across counties in New York, and ask which communities we measure most and least reliably. I have chosen to look at the median gross rent people pay in New York as the state has the highest average rental costs in the world. I’m curious to see how this average changes across different counties and regions of the state.

my_state <- "36"        # two-letter abbreviation, in quotes
my_variable <- "B25064_001"     # the variable code, in quotes

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
text:
Is the margin of error bigger in small places?

county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

head(county_wide)

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  GEOID NAME                         myvarE myvarM    popE  popM
  <chr> <chr>                         <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>
1 36001 Albany County, New York        1252     22  315374    NA
2 36003 Allegany County, New York       754     33   47027    NA
3 36005 Bronx County, New York         1436     11 1419250    NA
4 36007 Broome County, New York         914     26  197738    NA
5 36009 Cattaraugus County, New York    759     30   76479    NA
6 36011 Cayuga County, New York         895     39   75464    NA



county_wide <- county_wide %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 10 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

Now compare the average population of counties in each reliability category.

county_wide %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE)
  )

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  reliability     n_counties avg_population
  <chr>                <int>          <dbl>
1 High confidence         51        381479.
2 Low confidence           1          5102 
3 Moderate                10         41178.


Based on the size of the margin of error relative to its estimate (moe_pct), three buckets of reliability were created: high confidence (moe_pct<5), moderate confidence (moe_pct<10) and low confidence (moe_pct>=10). 51 counties fall into high confidence, 10 into moderate and 1 into low confidence.
A clear pattern can be observed across the three buckets: as me move from high to moderate to low confidence, the average population of these counties also falls.
Specifically, the average population of high confidence counties is 381,479, 41,178 for moderate confidence counties, and 5,102 for the low confidence one.
The data seems to suggest that smaller counties may be more likely to have higher margin of error relative to the underlying estimate.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy
When looking at county-wise median gross rental payments in the state of New York, we know the least about Hamilton County. This is based on the size of the margin of error relative to its corresponding estimate. Hamilton County has both the highest margin of error in absolute terms and the highest margin of error relative to the estimate: an MOE of 95 and an MOE of 11% relative to the estimate.
This is a function of its small population size and the sampling strategy used in the ACS. Data for the present analysis is drawn from ACS, which is based on sample surveys. These surveys draw smaller samples from less populous counties and larger samples from more populous ones. Counties such as Putnam County or Greene County have an MOE of 80 and 79, respectively, but their MOE percentages are 4.4 and 7.96, respectively. While their MOEs are 84% (Putnam) and 83% (Greene) of Hamilton’s, their MOE percentages are only 40% and 72% of Hamilton. This is because their respective populations are substantially bigger than Hamilton’s 5,102 people – with Putnam at 97,988 and Greene at 48,554.
If the state of New York or federal agencies were to use data from the ACS to devise policies related to rental housing, then it could be very inaccurate for smaller counties such as Hamilton County. Specifically, if the estimate reflects the lower end of the true rent being paid in Hamilton, then policies would end up underserving people who pay higher rents. Thus, before any action is taken, it would be advisable to conduct specific surveys in smaller counties or triangulate the estimate with county-specific administrative data.

title: Verify the Claim: Philly Neighbourhood Poverty Rate
text:
We will first load the requisite ACS data. As the article uses Five-Year Estimates for 2006-10 and 2013-17, we will call for the ACS5 data for these two survey periods.
The 2017 dataset has a poverty rate variable, “S1701_C03_001”, but that variable does not exist in the 2010 dataset. Accordingly, we will calculate the tract-wise poverty rate as a ratio of the count of people below the poverty line (B17001_002) to the count of people for whom poverty status is determined (B17001_001). The denominator cannot be total population, as that would bias the rate downwards by including people the Census Bureau excludes from the poverty universe, such as those in institutional group quarters.
We assume the article constructed a comparable poverty rate in this manner, since a common poverty rate variable does not exist across the two periods.
The two time periods used in the article do not overlap, which is a good thing. Since ACS5 estimates are averages over the five years covered, overlapping survey periods would share years of underlying data, and the two estimates could not be treated as independent. Here, 2011 and 2012 separate the two windows, so no respondent appears in both.
Lastly, the data will be called in a wide format so that each tract in a given year has separate columns for the poverty and total counts. Since we are stacking data from two rounds, the data will then be pivoted wider again so that each tract is a single row with separate columns for the two time periods.


Show code
philly2010 <- get_acs(geography = "tract", variables = c(below = "B17001_002", total = "B17001_001"),
  state = "PA", county = "Philadelphia",  year = 2010, survey = "acs5", output = "wide")

philly2017 <- get_acs(geography = "tract", variables = c(below = "B17001_002", total = "B17001_001"),
  state = "PA", county = "Philadelphia",  year = 2017, survey = "acs5", output = "wide")

philly <- bind_rows("2010" = philly2010, "2017" = philly2017, .id = "year")

phillywide <- pivot_wider(philly, id_cols = GEOID, names_from = year, values_from = c(belowE, belowM, totalE, totalM))


We have loaded the data required to (almost) replicate the analysis. Before beginning, let us take a look at the broad characteristics of our dataset.


Show code
philly %>%
  count(year) %>%
  kable(col.names = c("ACS 5-year period", "Census tracts"),
        caption = "Table 1. Census tracts retrieved for each survey period, Philadelphia County")

title: Verify the Claim: Philly Neighbourhood Poverty Rate
text:
Part 2
We first compute each tract’s poverty rate and the margin of error of that rate. The margin of error of a proportion does not carry over from the margin of error of the count, because both the numerator and the denominator are themselves estimates. moe_prop() implements the Census Bureau’s formula for combining them.


Show code
phillywide <- phillywide %>% 
  mutate(povpropE10 = belowE_2010/totalE_2010,
         povpropE17 = belowE_2017/totalE_2017,
         povpropM10 = moe_prop(belowE_2010, totalE_2010, belowM_2010, totalM_2010),
         povpropM17 = moe_prop(belowE_2017, totalE_2017, belowM_2017, totalM_2017))


The table below reports the unweighted mean of the tract-level rates. This is not the citywide poverty rate, and the difference matters. Averaging tract rates gives a 200-person tract the same weight as an 8,000-person tract. The correct citywide figure, computed by aggregating counts before dividing, appears in Part 3.


Show code
phillywide %>%
  summarise("2006-10" = round(mean(povpropE10, na.rm = TRUE)*100, 2),
            "2013-17" = round(mean(povpropE17, na.rm = TRUE)*100, 2)) %>%
  kable(caption = "Table 2. Unweighted mean of tract-level poverty rates (%), shown for comparison only")



Table 2. Unweighted mean of tract-level poverty rates (%), shown for comparison only


2006-10
2013-17




25.46
26.15





The coefficient of variation is calculated by dividing the standard error by the estimate and multiplying by 100 to turn it into a percentage. The ACS publishes margins of error at the 90% confidence level, which corresponds to a z-value of 1.645. We therefore calculate the standard error first by dividing the MOE by the z-value, then divide that by the estimate, and finally multiply by 100.


Show code
phillywide <- phillywide %>%
  mutate(cv10 = ((povpropM10/1.645)/povpropE10)*100,
         cv17 = ((povpropM17/1.645)/povpropE17)*100)


Along with computing the coefficient of variation, we categorise tracts by reliability using the Jurjevich et al. (2018) thresholds.


Show code
phillywide <- phillywide %>%
  mutate(reliability10 = case_when(
           cv10<12            ~ "Reliable",
           cv10>=12 & cv10<40 ~ "Somewhat reliable",
           cv10>=40           ~ "Unreliable",
           is.na(cv10)        ~ "Missing"),
         reliability17 = case_when(
           cv17<12            ~ "Reliable",
           cv17>=12 & cv17<40 ~ "Somewhat reliable",
           cv17>=40           ~ "Unreliable",
           is.na(cv17)        ~ "Missing")
  )



Reliability estimates
The table below shows how the tracts are distributed across the reliability classes. On the positive side, the share of unreliable tracts roughly halved between the two periods. On the negative, the share of tracts with genuinely reliable estimates remains very low: under 6 percent even in the later period. Seven tracts in 2006-10 and eight in 2013-17 have no computable rate at all.
One caution about the coefficient of variation: because it divides the margin of error by the estimate itself, a tract with a low poverty rate will appear unreliable even when its margin of error is modest in percentage-point terms. Part of the apparent improvement between the two periods may therefore reflect rising poverty rates rather than better precision.


Show code
reltable <- bind_rows(
  phillywide %>% count(Reliability = reliability10) %>% mutate(Period = "n2006"),
  phillywide %>% count(Reliability = reliability17) %>% mutate(Period = "n2013")
) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = Period, values_from = n) %>%
  mutate(Reliability = factor(Reliability,
           levels = c("Reliable", "Somewhat reliable", "Unreliable", "Missing"))) %>%

  mutate(Flag = case_when(Reliability == "Reliable"          ~ "+++",
                          Reliability == "Somewhat reliable" ~ "++",

Computing the change between the two periods and the margin of error of that change
We now investigate whether the poverty rate changed between the two periods, and if it did, whether the change is statistically significant or the kind of movement we might expect from sampling variation alone. There are three parts to this: first we estimate the change; second we calculate the margin of error of that change, following official Census Bureau guidance1; and third we test whether the change is distinguishable from zero.
The margin of error of a difference is the square root of the sum of the squared margins of error. Note that the squares are added even though the estimates are subtracted, because uncertainty accumulates in either operation. Since the 1.645 factors cancel, margins of error can be substituted directly for standard errors in this formula.


Show code
# Step 1: Estimating change in poverty rate
phillywide$povratechangeE = phillywide$povpropE17 - phillywide$povpropE10

# Step 2: Calculating the new MOE
phillywide$povratechangeM = sqrt(phillywide$povpropM10^2 + phillywide$povpropM17^2)

Testing whether the change is statistically significant
On a naive reading, the poverty rate at the tract level rose on average by 0.65 percentage points between the two ACS5 rounds. At the extremes, one tract shows an increase of 35.7 percentage points and another a drop of 78.8 points. The question is whether these movements reflect real change or sampling variation: if the ACS had happened to sample different households in each tract, would the estimates have come out very differently? To answer this, we implement a z-test.


Show code
phillywide <- phillywide %>%
  mutate(
    ztest = povratechangeE/(povratechangeM/1.645),
    siglevel = if_else(ztest > 1.645 | ztest < -1.645, 1, 0)
  )

count(phillywide, siglevel)


# A tibble: 3 × 2
  siglevel     n
     <dbl> <int>
1        0   313
2        1    63
3       NA     8


The test shows that 63 tracts (~17%) out of 376 with valid poverty data in both periods register a change distinguishable from zero at 90% confidence. Among those 63, the rate increased in 36 tracts and decreased in 27, so the detectable movement runs in both directions.


Show code
phillywide %>%
  filter(siglevel == 1) %>%
  mutate(Direction = if_else(povratechangeE > 0, "Increase", "Decrease")) %>%
  count(Direction) %>%

title: Verify the Claim: Philly Neighbourhood Poverty Rate
text:
Part 3: Adjudicate
We now sort the article’s claims into three buckets: supported, not supported, and undetermined.
Supported. The city’s 26 percent poverty rate for 2013-17 holds up. Aggregating counts across all tracts before dividing gives 25.8 percent, with a margin of error of plus or minus 0.5 percentage points. That interval is far tighter than any individual tract’s, because a citywide estimate pools the entire sample. The article’s characterisation of Philadelphia as a high-poverty city is accurate.


Show code

  summarise("2006-10 rate" = round(rate10*100, 2),
            "2006-10 MOE" = round(rate10_moe*100, 2),
            "2013-17 rate" = round(rate17*100, 2),
            "2013-17 MOE" = round(rate17_moe*100, 2),
            "Change" = round(change*100, 2),
            "MOE of change" = round(change_moe*100, 2),
            "Z-value" = round(z, 2)) %>%
  kable(caption = "Table 5. Citywide poverty rate, Philadelphia, in percent and percentage points. Rates are computed by aggregating tract counts, not by averaging tract rates. Margins of error are at 90% confidence, and a z-value above 1.645 would indicate a change distinguishable from zero.")

Not supported. The article opens by describing a city “still not recovered from the Great Recession” and quotes an economist on poverty continuing to rise robustly. The data do not show a rise. The citywide rate moved from 25.1 percent in 2006-10 to 25.8 percent in 2013-17, an increase of 0.72 percentage points against a margin of error of plus or minus 0.74 points. The resulting z-value of 1.60 falls short of the 1.645 threshold for 90 percent confidence, so the change cannot be distinguished from sampling variation. The defensible finding is that poverty stayed high, not that it worsened.
The tract-level picture is likewise mixed rather than uniformly deteriorating. Of the 376 tracts with a defined rate in both periods, only 63 (17 percent) show a change distinguishable from zero. The median tract moved 1.1 percentage points against a median margin of error of plus or minus 12.7 points. Among the 63 detectable changes, 36 were increases and 27 were decreases. The article’s description of Eastwick as showing “the greatest poverty-rate increase of any community” is a ranking claim, and rankings are the first thing to break under uncertainty of this magnitude: with error bars this wide, the data cannot identify a single worst-affected place.
Undetermined. Every named-neighborhood figure is unverifiable. The Inquirer aggregated census tracts into neighborhoods of its own drawing and never published which tracts went into which neighborhood, so Fairhill’s 61 percent and Eastwick’s rise from 12 to 26 percent can be neither reproduced nor falsified. Any boundary drawn here would be my construction rather than theirs.
The Holmesburg (2 to 19 percent) and Mayfair (1 to 14 percent) figures carry an additional ambiguity. Both appear in a section about white poverty, which suggests they are white-alone rates drawn from table B17001A rather than the overall rates used elsewhere in the article. A 2 percent overall poverty rate for a Philadelphia neighborhood would be implausible. The article never specifies which measure it is using, so the claims cannot be evaluated.
Finally, the income comparisons mix survey vintages. A 2013-17 five-year median of $39,759 is set against “$41,449 between 2016 and 2017,” and a one-year 2016-to-2017 white poverty figure is folded into an argument otherwise built on five-year estimates. Estimates from different ACS products are not directly comparable, and without knowing which series the article intends, the comparison cannot be assessed.

title: Verify the Claim: Philly Neighbourhood Poverty Rate
text:
Part 4 — Rewrite
A new federal survey finds that roughly one in four Philadelphians lived in poverty between 2013 and 2017, a rate that has barely moved since the years spanning the Great Recession. The citywide figure is solid. The neighborhood-level story is harder to pin down.
The American Community Survey reaches only a small sample in any one census tract, so estimates for small areas carry wide margins of error, typically around 13 percentage points when two periods are compared. Of 376 Philadelphia tracts, only 63 show a change large enough to separate from sampling noise, and those run in both directions. Some areas clearly got poorer; others clearly improved; most cannot be told apart from where they started.
Poverty in Philadelphia remains stubbornly high. Which specific blocks are worst off, and which are sliding fastest, is a question this data answers less confidently than the numbers suggest.

title: Assignment: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
Part 1: Choose your outcome
The outcome is the share of households with no vehicle available, built from table B08201. The numerator is households with no vehicle (B08201_002) and the denominator is all households (B08201_001). Using households rather than total population as the denominator matters for the same reason the poverty universe mattered in Assignment 3: vehicle availability is recorded for households, so people in group quarters are not part of the universe, and dividing by total population would bias the rate downwards in tracts with dormitories or institutions.
For the baseline, we choose four ACS predictors that plausibly relate to car ownership without being built from it:

Median household income (B19013_001): a car is expensive to own, so lower-income households are more likely to go without one.
Share of households renting (B25003_003 / B25003_001): renters are concentrated in denser rowhouse and apartment neighbourhoods where parking is scarce and a car is less necessary.
Share of adults 25+ with a bachelor’s degree or higher (B15003_022 to _025): this separates two very different car-free populations, lower-income households who cannot afford a car and higher-educated downtown households who choose not to own one.
Median age (B01002_001): older residents and young adults have different mobility needs and licensing rates.

We deliberately leave out the share of workers commuting by transit, walking or cycling (B08301). These are strongly related to the outcome, but they largely measure the same constraint from the other side: a household without a car commutes by transit because it has no car. An agency trying to predict car-free households would very likely not have commute-mode data without also having vehicle data, so including it would fail the Rule 3 test.

1A: Pull your outcome and your baseline predictors

Answer: The outcome is the share of households in each tract with no vehicle available. A transit agency or the City’s Office of Transportation would want to predict it because car-free households depend entirely on transit, walking and cycling to reach jobs, groceries and health care, so knowing where they are guides where service cuts would hurt most and where new bus routes or bike-share stations would do the most good. Reliability is acceptable. Of the 388 tracts with households, 29 are high, 313 moderate and 46 low, with a median CV of 23.4%; a further 20 tracts have no households, so no rate exists for them. The 46 low-reliability tracts have a median car-free share of just 6.0%, yet their median margin of error is 5.1 percentage points, the smallest of the three groups (against 9.7 for moderate and 8.2 for high). The red line is what a linear model can see; the grey curve is what the data actually do. Where the two diverge, a transformation in Part 5 may help. Three things stand out. Income bends sharply: the car-free share falls steeply up to a median income of roughly $75,000 and is flat, or even rising slightly, above $100,000, which already suggests a log. Education is U-shaped: car-free shares are high in tracts with few graduates, lowest around 30%, and high again where most adults hold a degree. Part 3: Getting data from Philadelphia’s open data portal


Code
# Encode every special character (including the % in LIKE patterns), and retry
# a few times, because the Carto server occasionally drops a connection.
carto_url <- function(sql, format) {
  paste0("https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=", format,
         "&q=", URLencode(sql, reserved = TRUE))
}

with_retry <- function(f, tries = 3) {
  for (i in seq_len(tries)) {
    out <- tryCatch(f(), error = function(e) e)
    if (!inherits(out, "error")) return(out)
    message("Carto request failed (attempt ", i, "): ", conditionMessage(out))
    Sys.sleep(3 * i)
  }
  stop(out)
}

carto_get <- function(sql) with_retry(function() st_read(carto_url(sql, "GeoJSON"), quiet = TRUE))
carto_csv <- function(sql) with_retry(function() read_csv(carto_url(sql, "csv"), show_col_types = FALSE))

Answer: The baseline knows who lives in a tract but not what the streets look like. A car that does not exist cannot be stolen, broken into or abandoned, so vehicle-related crime and 311 complaints work as indirect counts of the cars present in a place, information the ACS predictors only capture through income. We expect motor vehicle theft and thefts from vehicles to be higher where more cars are parked on the street, and abandoned-vehicle complaints to mark neighbourhoods where car ownership is common enough that disused cars accumulate. Indego stations capture the opposite side: the availability of an alternative to driving.
Two caveats are worth stating up front. First, vehicle crime also reflects where people drive to, not only where they live: Center City has many thefts from vehicles because commuters and visitors park there, which may weaken the link to residents’ car ownership. Second, 2023 motor vehicle thefts were inflated by the Kia and Hyundai theft wave, which targeted particular models rather than places with more cars. Finally, the Indego feed returns today’s stations rather than the 2023 network, so it uses a little information from the future (Rule 2). Any stations opened since 2023 make this feature slightly optimistic; a historical station list would be the clean fix.

title: Assignment: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
Part 4: Building spatial features
We build the features once, then add them to the model one at a time so each row of the log isolates one change.


Code
tract_pts <- st_point_on_surface(tracts)

city_hall <- st_sfc(st_point(c(-75.1636, 39.9526)), crs = 4326) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))

nearest_idx <- st_nearest_feature(tract_pts, stations)

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    area_sqmi = as.numeric(st_area(.)) / 27878400,

    # counts
    n_veh_theft      = lengths(st_intersects(., veh_theft)),
    n_theft_from_veh = lengths(st_intersects(., theft_from_veh)),
    n_abandoned      = lengths(st_intersects(., abandoned)),

    # densities
    veh_theft_per_1k_hh  = n_veh_theft / hhE * 1000,
    theft_from_veh_sqmi  = n_theft_from_veh / area_sqmi,
    abandoned_per_1k_hh  = n_abandoned / hhE * 1000,
    pop_per_sqmi         = total_popE / area_sqmi,

    # distances
    dist_station_mi = as.numeric(
      st_distance(tract_pts, stations[nearest_idx, ], by_element = TRUE)) / 5280,
    dist_ch_mi = as.numeric(st_distance(tract_pts, city_hall)) / 5280
  )

tracts %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(veh_theft_per_1k_hh, theft_from_veh_sqmi, abandoned_per_1k_hh,

Answer: Distance to City Hall helped most. Added to the baseline on its own, it lowered CV RMSE from 12.44 to 10.27 points, a cut of 2.17; added in sequence after the Indego feature, it still took off a further 1.47. This fits the baseline residual map: the largest misses followed distance from the centre, and distance from the centre is a summary of everything that makes going without a car practical, from jobs and shops within walking distance to the densest transit service.
The comparison between the two tables is itself instructive. On its own, distance to the nearest Indego station cut CV RMSE by 1.14 and population density by 1.05, but in sequence density added only 0.16. All three features largely measure the same thing, centrality. The Indego network is concentrated in and around Center City (the median tract is a third of a mile from a station, but the mean is 1.7 miles and the furthest tract is 11 miles away), so outside the core, distance to the nearest station is mostly distance to the centre under another name.
The disappointment was the vehicle-crime and 311 layers. Motor vehicle thefts made the model slightly worse (CV RMSE rose by 0.03 on its own), and thefts from vehicles and abandoned-vehicle complaints each improved it by less than 0.05 points. We expected a car that does not exist to be impossible to steal, but two things got in the way. First, thefts from vehicles follow where cars are parked, which in the centre means commuters’ and shoppers’ cars rather than residents’. Second, 2023 was the peak of the Kia and Hyundai theft wave, so motor vehicle thefts track where particular models were parked rather than how many cars there were. A small rise in CV RMSE is itself a finding: a predictor that carries no new information still costs the model a parameter, and cross-validation penalises that where in-sample R² would not.

title: Assignment: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
Part 5: Transforming features
Following the October 9 lecture, the outcome stays in percentage points so every row of the log is comparable; only predictors are transformed. We start from the full m7 specification and change one thing at a time.

5A: Logs
The Part 2A plots showed income bending, and the Part 4 summary showed density and the crime rates are heavily right-skewed: most tracts have modest values and a handful have very large ones.


Code
tracts %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(med_income, pop_per_sqmi, veh_theft_per_1k_hh) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything()) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  facet_wrap(~ name, scales = "free") + theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Raw", x = NULL)









Code
tracts %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  transmute(log_income = log(med_income),
            log1p_density = log1p(pop_per_sqmi),
            log1p_veh_theft = log1p(veh_theft_per_1k_hh)) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything()) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  facet_wrap(~ name, scales = "free") + theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Logged", x = NULL)









Income is always positive, so it takes a plain log(). The density and crime rates can be zero, so they take log1p().


Code

swap <- function(spec, old, new) c(setdiff(spec, old), new)

spec_log_inc <- swap(spec7, "med_income", "log(med_income)")
model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m8", added = "log of median income",
          cv_rmse = cv_rmse(reformulate(spec_log_inc, response = "y"), tracts),
          notes = "replaces linear income in m7")

spec_log_dens <- swap(spec_log_inc, "pop_per_sqmi", "log1p(pop_per_sqmi)")
model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m9", added = "log1p of population density",
          cv_rmse = cv_rmse(reformulate(spec_log_dens, response = "y"), tracts),
          notes = "builds on m8")

  swap("veh_theft_per_1k_hh", "log1p(veh_theft_per_1k_hh)") %>%
  swap("abandoned_per_1k_hh", "log1p(abandoned_per_1k_hh)") %>%
  swap("theft_from_veh_sqmi", "log1p(theft_from_veh_sqmi)")
model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m10", added = "log1p of the three vehicle-crime/311 rates",
          cv_rmse = cv_rmse(reformulate(spec_log_crime, response = "y"), tracts),

Answer: The log of median income helped most, lowering CV RMSE from 9.62 to 9.22 points. This matches the scatterplot in Part 2A: the car-free share falls steeply across the lowest incomes and then flattens, so a straight line was overstating the effect of income among better-off tracts and understating it among the poorest. A log says that going from $20,000 to $40,000 matters as much as going from $60,000 to $120,000, which is closer to how car ownership actually works.
Not every log helped. Logging population density made the model worse (9.22 to 9.44), most likely because distance to City Hall was already capturing the shape of density’s effect, and compressing density’s upper tail removed the one thing it added: the difference between the very densest central tracts and the merely dense ones. These features did almost nothing as raw rates in Part 4 but earned their place once logged, because the log stopped a handful of extreme tracts from dominating their coefficients. The squared distance term took CV RMSE to 9.00, the best of any model. Its plot shows why: a straight line keeps falling until it predicts negative car-free shares at the city’s edge, while the curve levels off at around 5%, which is what the outer tracts actually show. The ring variable did worse (9.31) than the continuous distance it replaced. Three categories throw away the variation within each ring, and within the Core in particular, car-free shares range from about 20% to nearly 80%.
Reading the categorical variable, with Core (within two miles of City Hall) as the reference level: holding income, tenure, education, age, density and the vehicle-crime features constant, a tract in the Outer ring is predicted to have about 15.0 percentage points fewer households without a car than an otherwise similar tract in the Core (and an Inner tract about 8.3 points fewer).

title: Assignment: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
Part 7: Reflection
The feature that helped most was distance to City Hall, which on its own cut the baseline’s error by more than two points. The reason is the one the baseline residual map pointed to: the model knew who lived in a tract but not where. Income and tenure explain why a household might not afford a car; centrality explains whether it can manage without one. The most disappointing was motor vehicle theft, the only feature that made the model worse on its own. We expected car crime to stand in for car ownership, but in 2023 it mostly measured where Kias and Hyundais were parked. Vehicle crime did eventually earn a place, but only once logged, which says the signal was there and was being drowned out by a few extreme tracts.
Reading one coefficient twice: in the final model, the coefficient on log median income is β̂ = −14.8. As a β̂ reading, a 1% increase in a tract’s median income is associated with about 0.15 percentage points fewer car-free households, holding the other predictors constant. As a ŷ reading, the model predicts that of two otherwise identical tracts, one with a median income of $40,000 and one with $80,000, the richer tract would have about 10.3 percentage points fewer households without a car.
What’s still missing is transit access. The red band that survives in North Philadelphia is a set of tracts the model treats like their neighbours, but it appears to follow the Broad Street corridor, where a subway line makes life without a car far easier than distance from City Hall would suggest. Distance to the nearest Indego station is only a partial stand-in. SEPTA publishes its full schedule as GTFS, from which one could count trips per day at stops within a quarter mile of each tract, measuring not just whether transit exists but whether it comes often enough to live on.
Some of the remaining error is not the model’s fault at all. The final model misses the median tract by 5.4 percentage points, while the median margin of error on the outcome itself is 9.0 points, and 70% of tracts are predicted within their own margin of error. For most tracts, then, the model’s miss is smaller than the survey’s own uncertainty about the true value. The fog plot, however, shows no clear relationship between a tract’s CV and the size of its miss. The largest misses, of 20 to 27 points, sit among tracts with CVs between 10% and 35%, and the wiggles in the smoothed line at high CVs are driven by a handful of points. So noise accounts for much of the typical error, and lowering CV RMSE much further would partly mean fitting noise, but the biggest misses are real failures of the model in tracts we measure reasonably well. Those are where the next feature should be aimed.

Part 0: Setup (provided)
These helpers are to help you get off the ground.


Code
check_na <- function(formula, df) {
  vars <- all.vars(formula)
  bad <- vars[sapply(vars, function(v) any(is.na(df[[v]])))]
  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    stop("These variables have NAs: ", paste(bad, collapse = ", "),
         ". Fill them or choose another variable (Rule 1).")
  }
}

# 10-fold CV RMSE, same folds every time
cv_rmse <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  check_na(formula, df)
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm",
               trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10))
  fit$results$RMSE
}

# Each house's prediction from the fold where it was held out
cv_pred <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  check_na(formula, df)
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm",
               trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10,
                                        savePredictions = "final"))
  fit$pred %>% arrange(rowIndex) %>% pull(pred)
}

# Chicago Data Portal (Socrata) -> sf. `where` is a SoQL filter.
socrata_get <- function(dataset, where, select = NULL, limit = 200000) {
  where <- str_squish(where)
  q <- paste0("$where=", URLencode(where, reserved = TRUE), "&$limit=", limit)
  if (!is.null(select)) q <- paste0(q, "&$select=", URLencode(str_squish(select), reserved = TRUE))
  url <- paste0("https://data.cityofchicago.org/resource/", dataset, ".geojson?", q)
  tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".geojson")
  resp <- tryCatch(download.file(url, tmp, quiet = TRUE), error = function(e) e)
  if (inherits(resp, "error")) stop("Portal request failed. Open this URL in a browser to see why:\n", url)
  st_read(tmp, quiet = TRUE)
}

Answer: What in your exploration shaped your modeling choices?
Your answer:
Our five cleaning rules removed 39 of 23,200 training sales (see the table above): 30 sales of $5 million or more, 8 homes with more than 4 fireplaces and 1 lot over 3 acres. We checked for $1 transfers and negative ages and found none (the cheapest sale is about $10,000). We kept rows with missing values and filled them instead, and we kept new construction (age 0).
Our first draft also dropped every sale over $1 million. The histogram changed our minds: those 1,892 sales are 8.2% of the training data, not a few outliers, and the test houses are not cleaned, so the model has to price them. Dropping them made CV RMSE look good only because the hardest homes were gone. We now drop only the top 0.1% (over $5 million).
Two other things from the plots shaped the model. The price map shows a clear north/south split, with higher prices on the North Side and near the lake. A model built only on house features cannot see that, so we knew we would need location features. And the age plot is U-shaped: new homes sell highest, prices bottom out for homes 50–100 years old, and rise again for the oldest (historic) homes. So we added age squared.

4A. The model fails worst along the North Side lakefront. Lincoln Park, Near North Side and Lake View have the largest average errors of any community area (about $622,000 per home in Lincoln Park, where the median sale is $1.6 million). Every community area’s average residual is close to zero, because the community-area fixed effect absorbs it. The errors show up inside these neighborhoods, and they go in both directions:

Too low in tracts where the most expensive homes sell, such as parts of Lake View, Lincoln Park and West Town (median sales around $1.7–3.3 million). In the worst tract, in Lincoln Park (median sale $3.3 million), homes sold for about $655,000 more than predicted on average.
Too high in other tracts of the same neighborhoods, such as parts of Lincoln Park and the Near North Side, where homes are cheaper for the area (median around $0.8–1.3 million). In the worst tract, homes sold for about $605,000 less than predicted on average. The same thing happens far from the lakefront: in one Greater Grand Crossing tract, where the median sale is $70,000, homes sold for about $347,000 less than predicted.

We think this happens because the community-area fixed effect gives every home in a neighborhood the same location premium. In most of the city that works, because prices within a neighborhood are similar. On the North Side lakefront, prices range from under $1 million to over $4 million, and nothing in our model tells a $3 million home from a $900,000 one on the next block except its size, age and lot. So the model pushes both toward the neighborhood average: the top-end homes are under-valued and the more modest ones are over-valued.
4B. Only slightly, and not in the direction we expected. In the final model, the median ratio is 0.93 for homes in the lowest-income fifth of tracts and 1.03 in the highest, rising fairly steadily in between. If anything, homes in richer tracts are slightly over-valued. At the tract level, the poverty coefficient is −0.0040 (p < 0.001): each one-point rise in a tract’s poverty rate lowers its median ratio by about 0.4%. Poverty explains under 3% of the variation in tract ratios (R² = 0.027). In our first draft, which had no location features, the same regression gave a coefficient of +0.026, with ratios rising about 2.6% per point of poverty. Adding tract income and poverty to the model removed that neighborhood-level bias, because the model now knows which neighborhoods are poorer.
The pattern by sale price is a different story. The cheapest tenth of homes have a median ratio of 1.88, while the most expensive tenth have 0.92. This is the same pattern “The Tax Divide” found in Cook County: lower-value homes are assessed at a higher share of their worth. Our location features fixed the bias between neighborhoods, but not the bias between cheap and expensive homes within them.
Our cleaning rules connect to this in both directions. At the top, our first draft dropped every sale over $1 million, which hid the expensive end of the market; keeping those sales gave the model a more honest view of it. At the bottom, we kept every sale, including about 170 sales under $30,000. Some of these may be foreclosures or other distressed sales rather than true market sales, and they push the ratio for the cheapest decile up sharply. We had no rule that could tell them apart from real low-priced sales, so we left them in. An Assessor faces the same choice. If this model were used for assessments, owners of the cheapest homes would be over-assessed the most, and they would pay a larger share of the tax bill.

Part 6: Reflection (about 300 words, as a team)

Read one coefficient twice: once as β̂, once for what it does to ŷ.
Would you hand this model to the Assessor? What would you warn them about?

Your answer:
Our final model enters bedrooms as log1p(num_bedrooms). As β̂, the coefficient is −$43,883: the change in predicted price for a one-unit increase in log(1 + bedrooms), holding living area, age, lot size, fireplaces and location fixed. On its own that is hard to use, since nobody adds “one log unit” of bedrooms to a house.
For ŷ, going from 2 to 3 bedrooms raises log1p by log(4/3) ≈ 0.29, which lowers the prediction by about $12,600. Going from 4 to 5 bedrooms raises it by only log(6/5) ≈ 0.18, which lowers the prediction by about $8,000. Each extra bedroom matters less than the one before. Because living area is held fixed, the negative sign means that splitting the same space into more, smaller rooms lowers the predicted price.
We would not hand this model to the Assessor yet. Adding location cut CV RMSE from $301,503 to $219,363, but three problems remain. First, Moran’s I is still 0.263, so errors are still clustered: on the North Side lakefront, whole blocks of top-end homes are under-valued while their cheaper neighbors are over-valued. Second, the model is regressive. The cheapest tenth of homes are predicted at 1.88 times their sale price and the most expensive tenth at 0.92, which is the “Tax Divide” pattern. Adding location removed the bias by neighborhood poverty, but not this one: owners of cheaper homes, in every part of the city, would get relatively higher tax bills. Third, a linear model in dollars can predict prices that make no sense: 110 test homes were predicted below $10,000 (some below zero) and had to be set to a floor.
Before using it, we would add features that capture variation inside neighborhoods (transit access, crime, distance to the lake) and test the ratio by price and income again after every change.

check_na <- function(formula, df) {
  vars <- all.vars(formula)
  bad <- vars[sapply(vars, function(v) any(is.na(df[[v]])))]
  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    stop("These variables have NAs: ", paste(bad, collapse = ", "),
         ". Fill them or choose another variable (Rule 1).")
  }
}

# 10-fold CV RMSE, same folds every time
cv_rmse <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  check_na(formula, df)
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm",
               trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10))
  fit$results$RMSE
}

# Each house's prediction from the fold where it was held out
cv_pred <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  check_na(formula, df)
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm",
               trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10,
                                        savePredictions = "final"))
  fit$pred %>% arrange(rowIndex) %>% pull(pred)
}

# Chicago Data Portal (Socrata) -> sf. `where` is a SoQL filter.
socrata_get <- function(dataset, where, select = NULL, limit = 200000) {
  where <- str_squish(where)
  q <- paste0("$where=", URLencode(where, reserved = TRUE), "&$limit=", limit)
  if (!is.null(select)) q <- paste0(q, "&$select=", URLencode(str_squish(select), reserved = TRUE))
  url <- paste0("https://data.cityofchicago.org/resource/", dataset, ".geojson?", q)
  tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".geojson")
  resp <- tryCatch(download.file(url, tmp, quiet = TRUE), error = function(e) e)
  if (inherits(resp, "error")) stop("Portal request failed. Open this URL in a browser to see why:\n", url)

Answer: What in your exploration shaped your modeling choices?
Your answer:
Our five cleaning rules removed 39 of 23,200 training sales (see the table above): 30 sales of $5 million or more, 8 homes with more than 4 fireplaces and 1 lot over 3 acres. We checked for $1 transfers and negative ages and found none (the cheapest sale is about $10,000). We kept rows with missing values and filled them instead, and we kept new construction (age 0).
Our first draft also dropped every sale over $1 million. The histogram changed our minds: those 1,892 sales are 8.2% of the training data, not a few outliers, and the test houses are not cleaned, so the model has to price them. Dropping them made CV RMSE look good only because the hardest homes were gone. We now drop only the top 0.1% (over $5 million).
Two other things from the plots shaped the model. The price map shows a clear north/south split, with higher prices on the North Side and near the lake. A model built only on house features cannot see that, so we knew we would need location features. And the age plot is U-shaped: new homes sell highest, prices bottom out for homes 50–100 years old, and rise again for the oldest (historic) homes. So we added age squared.

  mutate(num_fireplaces = replace_na(num_fireplaces, 0),
         building_000sf = replace_na(building_000sf, median(building_000sf, na.rm = TRUE)),
         building_age   = replace_na(building_age,   median(building_age,   na.rm = TRUE)),
         lotsize_acre   = replace_na(lotsize_acre,   median(lotsize_acre,   na.rm = TRUE)),
         num_bedrooms   = replace_na(num_bedrooms,   median(num_bedrooms,   na.rm = TRUE)))

# Feature 1: distance to the Loop (State & Madison), in miles

all_sales <- all_sales %>%
  mutate(dist_loop_mi = as.numeric(st_distance(geometry, loop)) / 5280)

# Feature 2: census tract income and poverty (ACS 2023 5-year)

  geography = "tract", state = "IL", county = "Cook", year = 2023,
  variables = c(med_inc = "B19013_001",
                pov     = "B17001_002",
                pov_den = "B17001_001"),     # population for whom poverty is determined
  geometry = TRUE, output = "wide") %>%
  mutate(med_inc = med_incE,
         pct_pov = 100 * povE / pov_denE) %>%
  select(GEOID, med_inc, pct_pov) %>%
  st_transform(3435)

  st_join(acs, join = st_nearest_feature) %>%
  mutate(med_inc = replace_na(med_inc, median(med_inc, na.rm = TRUE)),
         pct_pov = replace_na(pct_pov, median(pct_pov, na.rm = TRUE)))

  select(community) %>%
  st_transform(3435)

  st_join(ca, join = st_nearest_feature)

Answer: What helped most, and what disappointed you? Use your log.
Your answer:
Location helped most. The structure-only baseline (m1) had a CV RMSE of $301,503 and a Moran’s I of 0.455. The house-feature steps (m2–m4: bedrooms, fireplaces, logged bedrooms, age squared) only brought CV RMSE down to $288,721, about $12,800 in total. The three location steps together cut it by almost $70,000. The community-area fixed effect (m7) was the biggest single step, cutting CV RMSE by about $36,700 and Moran’s I from 0.422 to 0.263. Tract income and poverty (m6) came second, cutting CV RMSE by about $24,600; distance to the Loop (m5) added about $8,000. Our final model (m7) has a CV RMSE of $219,363 and a Moran’s I of 0.263.
Three things disappointed us. Logging bedrooms, which we expected to help, changed CV RMSE by less than $600. Distance to the Loop lowered CV RMSE but slightly raised Moran’s I (0.459 to 0.476), so on its own it did not fix the clustering. And even the final model leaves Moran’s I well above zero, so nearby homes are still wrong in the same direction.
The residual maps show what changed. In the baseline map, a large red cluster runs along the North Side lakefront (Lincoln Park, Lake View, North Center): the model under-predicts the city’s most expensive area because it does not know where homes are. In the final map, most of the city is close to zero and that north/south pattern is gone. The large errors that remain are still along the North Side lakefront, but now in both directions, with red and blue points next to each other. The model now knows the neighborhood, but not which homes within it are the top-end ones.

Your answers:
4A. The model fails worst along the North Side lakefront. Lincoln Park, Near North Side and Lake View have the largest average errors of any community area (about $622,000 per home in Lincoln Park, where the median sale is $1.6 million). Every community area’s average residual is close to zero, because the community-area fixed effect absorbs it. The errors show up inside these neighborhoods, and they go in both directions:

Too low in tracts where the most expensive homes sell, such as parts of Lake View, Lincoln Park and West Town (median sales around $1.7–3.3 million). In the worst tract, in Lincoln Park (median sale $3.3 million), homes sold for about $655,000 more than predicted on average.
Too high in other tracts of the same neighborhoods, such as parts of Lincoln Park and the Near North Side, where homes are cheaper for the area (median around $0.8–1.3 million). In the worst tract, homes sold for about $605,000 less than predicted on average. The same thing happens far from the lakefront: in one Greater Grand Crossing tract, where the median sale is $70,000, homes sold for about $347,000 less than predicted.

We think this happens because the community-area fixed effect gives every home in a neighborhood the same location premium. In most of the city that works, because prices within a neighborhood are similar. On the North Side lakefront, prices range from under $1 million to over $4 million, and nothing in our model tells a $3 million home from a $900,000 one on the next block except its size, age and lot. So the model pushes both toward the neighborhood average: the top-end homes are under-valued and the more modest ones are over-valued.
4B. Only slightly, and not in the direction we expected. In the final model, the median ratio is 0.93 for homes in the lowest-income fifth of tracts and 1.03 in the highest, rising fairly steadily in between. If anything, homes in richer tracts are slightly over-valued. At the tract level, the poverty coefficient is −0.0040 (p < 0.001): each one-point rise in a tract’s poverty rate lowers its median ratio by about 0.4%. Poverty explains under 3% of the variation in tract ratios (R² = 0.027). In our first draft, which had no location features, the same regression gave a coefficient of +0.026, with ratios rising about 2.6% per point of poverty. Adding tract income and poverty to the model removed that neighborhood-level bias, because the model now knows which neighborhoods are poorer.
The pattern by sale price is a different story. The cheapest tenth of homes have a median ratio of 1.88, while the most expensive tenth have 0.92. This is the same pattern “The Tax Divide” found in Cook County: lower-value homes are assessed at a higher share of their worth. Our location features fixed the bias between neighborhoods, but not the bias between cheap and expensive homes within them.
Our cleaning rules connect to this in both directions. At the top, our first draft dropped every sale over $1 million, which hid the expensive end of the market; keeping those sales gave the model a more honest view of it. At the bottom, we kept every sale, including about 170 sales under $30,000. Some of these may be foreclosures or other distressed sales rather than true market sales, and they push the ratio for the cheapest decile up sharply. We had no rule that could tell them apart from real low-priced sales, so we left them in. An Assessor faces the same choice. If this model were used for assessments, owners of the cheapest homes would be over-assessed the most, and they would pay a larger share of the tax bill.

Part 6: Reflection (about 300 words, as a team)

Read one coefficient twice: once as β̂, once for what it does to ŷ.
Would you hand this model to the Assessor? What would you warn them about?

Your answer:
Our final model enters bedrooms as log1p(num_bedrooms). As β̂, the coefficient is −$43,883: the change in predicted price for a one-unit increase in log(1 + bedrooms), holding living area, age, lot size, fireplaces and location fixed. On its own that is hard to use, since nobody adds “one log unit” of bedrooms to a house.
For ŷ, going from 2 to 3 bedrooms raises log1p by log(4/3) ≈ 0.29, which lowers the prediction by about $12,600. Going from 4 to 5 bedrooms raises it by only log(6/5) ≈ 0.18, which lowers the prediction by about $8,000. Each extra bedroom matters less than the one before. Because living area is held fixed, the negative sign means that splitting the same space into more, smaller rooms lowers the predicted price.
We would not hand this model to the Assessor yet. Adding location cut CV RMSE from $301,503 to $219,363, but three problems remain. First, Moran’s I is still 0.263, so errors are still clustered: on the North Side lakefront, whole blocks of top-end homes are under-valued while their cheaper neighbors are over-valued. Second, the model is regressive. The cheapest tenth of homes are predicted at 1.88 times their sale price and the most expensive tenth at 0.92, which is the “Tax Divide” pattern. Adding location removed the bias by neighborhood poverty, but not this one: owners of cheaper homes, in every part of the city, would get relatively higher tax bills. Third, a linear model in dollars can predict prices that make no sense: 110 test homes were predicted below $10,000 (some below zero) and had to be set to a floor.
Before using it, we would add features that capture variation inside neighborhoods (transit access, crime, distance to the lake) and test the ratio by price and income again after every change.
